item.title: Flux Balance Analysis of E. coli Central Metabolism: Growth, Knockouts, and Nutrient Shifts
item.dc:creator: Peekei
item.description:
1. Motivation

A genome-scale metabolic model (GEM) is a stoichiometric reconstruction of every known biochemical reaction an organism’s genome can catalyse — thousands of reactions connected through shared metabolites, each reaction tied back to the gene or genes that encode its enzyme. That structure alone doesn’t predict behaviour. Flux Balance Analysis (FBA) turns the structure into a prediction by assuming the cell is at metabolic steady state and solving a linear program: find the distribution of reaction fluxes that maximises a chosen objective (almost always growth, represented as flux through a biomass reaction) subject to the stoichiometric constraints and the uptake bounds available in the environment.

What makes this genuinely useful rather than a curve-fitting exercise is that the model is mechanistic — asking “what happens if gene X is knocked out” is answered by removing every reaction that gene uniquely catalyses and re-solving the same optimisation, not by fitting a new statistical relationship. This piece works through baseline FBA on E. coli’s core metabolic model, the degeneracy problem that plain FBA has and how parsimonious FBA (pFBA) resolves it, flux variability analysis, growth response to different carbon sources and oxygen availability, and systematic single- and double-gene knockout screening.

2. Model Acquisition

Show code 
import os
import gzip
import shutil
import time
import urllib.request

import cobra
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_style("whitegrid")

MODEL_PATH   = "e_coli_core.xml"
BIGG_URL_XML = "http://bigg.ucsd.edu/static/models/e_coli_core.xml"
BIGG_URL_GZ  = "http://bigg.ucsd.edu/static/models/e_coli_core.xml.gz"
MIN_VALID_SIZE = 400_000   # real file is ~700KB; anything much smaller is a truncated download

def is_valid_model_file(path):
    """A partial/corrupt download can pass os.path.exists() — check size
    and that it actually parses as XML before trusting it."""
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return False
    if os.path.getsize(path) < MIN_VALID_SIZE:
        return False
    try:
        with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") as f:
            head = f.read(200)
        return "<sbml" in head.lower() or "<?xml" in head.lower()
    except Exception:
        return False

def try_download(url, dest, attempts=3, timeout=30):
    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
        try:
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, dest)
            return True
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  Attempt {attempt}/{attempts} failed: {e}")
            if os.path.exists(dest):
                os.remove(dest)   # never leave a partial file behind
            if attempt < attempts:
                time.sleep(3)
    return False

# If a stale/partial file exists from an earlier interrupted run, discard it
if os.path.exists(MODEL_PATH) and not is_valid_model_file(MODEL_PATH):
    print("Found an incomplete or corrupt model file from a previous run — removing it.")
    os.remove(MODEL_PATH)

if not is_valid_model_file(MODEL_PATH):
    print("Downloading e_coli_core model from BiGG (uncompressed XML)...")
    success = try_download(BIGG_URL_XML, MODEL_PATH)

    if not success or not is_valid_model_file(MODEL_PATH):
        print("Uncompressed download failed — trying gzipped version...")
        gz_path = MODEL_PATH + ".gz"
        success = try_download(BIGG_URL_GZ, gz_path)
        if success:
            with gzip.open(gz_path, "rb") as f_in, open(MODEL_PATH, "wb") as f_out:
                shutil.copyfileobj(f_in, f_out)
            os.remove(gz_path)

    if not is_valid_model_file(MODEL_PATH):
        raise RuntimeError(
            "\n\nCould not download the model automatically after multiple attempts — "
            "this usually means a network or DNS issue on this machine rather than a "
            "problem with the code. To work around it:\n\n"
            "  1. Open this URL in your browser:\n"
            "     http://bigg.ucsd.edu/static/models/e_coli_core.xml\n"
            "  2. Save the file as 'e_coli_core.xml'\n"
            f"  3. Place it in the same folder as this .qmd file:\n"
            f"     {os.path.abspath('.')}\n"
            "  4. Re-render — the code will detect the file and skip downloading.\n"
        )
    else:
        print("Download succeeded.")
else:
    print("Using existing local model file (already downloaded).")

model = cobra.io.read_sbml_model(MODEL_PATH)

print(f"Reactions:  {len(model.reactions)}")
print(f"Metabolites:{len(model.metabolites)}")
print(f"Genes:      {len(model.genes)}")
print(f"Objective:  {model.objective.expression}")

Download succeeded.
Reactions:  95
Metabolites:72
Genes:      137
Objective:  1.0*BIOMASS_Ecoli_core_w_GAM - 1.0*BIOMASS_Ecoli_core_w_GAM_reverse_712e5

The E. coli core model is deliberately small — it captures glycolysis, the TCA cycle, the pentose phosphate pathway, oxidative phosphorylation, and central carbon exchange reactions, without the full genome-scale reconstruction’s thousands of peripheral reactions. That size is an advantage here: every result below can be inspected pathway-by-pathway rather than disappearing into a reaction list too large to reason about directly.

3. Baseline FBA and the Degeneracy Problem

Show code 
solution_fba = model.optimize()

print(f"Growth rate (FBA):  {solution_fba.objective_value:.4f} 1/h")
print(f"Status: {solution_fba.status}")
print(f"Sum of absolute fluxes (FBA solution): {solution_fba.fluxes.abs().sum():.2f}")
Growth rate (FBA):  0.8739 1/h
Status: optimal
Sum of absolute fluxes (FBA solution): 518.42

Plain FBA found a growth rate, but that number can correspond to more than one flux distribution. Whenever a metabolic network has redundant or parallel routes between the same start and end points — which real metabolism almost always does — many different flux vectors can achieve the identical optimal growth rate. Reporting “the” flux distribution from plain FBA without acknowledging this is misleading: the solver returned a solution, not necessarily a biologically representative one.

Parsimonious FBA (pFBA) resolves this by adding a second objective: among all flux distributions that achieve the optimal growth rate, find the one with the minimum total flux. This is motivated by the assumption that cells don’t run unnecessary enzymatic reactions when a leaner route achieves the same growth — an assumption with real biological support, not an arbitrary tie-breaker.

Show code 
solution_pfba = cobra.flux_analysis.pfba(model)

# IMPORTANT: pfba() internally swaps the model's objective to "minimize
# total flux" before re-solving, so solution_pfba.objective_value reflects
# THAT objective (the total flux sum) — not the growth rate. The growth
# rate has to be read back out as the flux through the biomass reaction
# specifically. Biomass reactions are identified by convention (their id
# contains "biomass") rather than assumed to have one fixed name, since
# that varies slightly across BiGG models.
biomass_reaction = next(r for r in model.reactions if "biomass" in r.id.lower())
pfba_growth_rate = solution_pfba.fluxes[biomass_reaction.id]

print(f"Biomass reaction: {biomass_reaction.id}")
print(f"Growth rate (pFBA): {pfba_growth_rate:.4f} 1/h")
print(f"Sum of absolute fluxes (pFBA solution): {solution_pfba.fluxes.abs().sum():.2f}")
Biomass reaction: BIOMASS_Ecoli_core_w_GAM
Growth rate (pFBA): 0.8739 1/h
Sum of absolute fluxes (pFBA solution): 518.42
WarningImplementation gotcha

pfba() re-solves the model against a different objective internally — total flux minimisation, subject to growth being fixed at its optimum — so the Solution.objective_value it returns reflects that internal flux-minimisation objective, not the growth rate. Reading .objective_value directly off a pFBA solution and assuming it’s the growth rate silently produces a nonsensical number (it would come out numerically identical to the total flux sum). The growth rate itself has to be read back out as the flux through the biomass reaction specifically, which is what the code above does.

Show code 
top_reactions = solution_pfba.fluxes.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(15).index

compare_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "FBA":  solution_fba.fluxes[top_reactions].abs(),
    "pFBA": solution_pfba.fluxes[top_reactions].abs()
})

compare_df.plot(kind="barh", figsize=(8, 6))
plt.xlabel("Absolute flux (mmol/gDCW/h)")
plt.ylabel("Reaction")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Both solutions achieve the same growth rate by construction, but the total flux carried differs — the gap between the two “sum of absolute fluxes” numbers above is the degeneracy plain FBA leaves unresolved. Every subsequent analysis in this piece uses the pFBA solution as the reference flux distribution for exactly this reason.

4. Flux Variability Analysis

FVA asks a different question than pFBA: rather than picking one flux distribution, what is the range each reaction’s flux can take while the network still achieves at least some specified fraction of the optimal growth rate? Reactions with a wide FVA range have genuine flexibility — the cell could reroute flux through them without cost. Reactions with a narrow or zero-width range are load-bearing: any deviation compromises growth.

Show code 
fva_result = cobra.flux_analysis.flux_variability_analysis(
    model, loopless="fastSNP", fraction_of_optimum=0.9
)
fva_result["range"] = fva_result["maximum"] - fva_result["minimum"]
fva_result_sorted = fva_result.sort_values("range", ascending=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
ax.barh(top_var.index, top_var["maximum"] - top_var["minimum"],
        left=top_var["minimum"], color="#4DBBD5", alpha=0.85)
ax.axvline(0, color="grey", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)

ax.set_ylabel("Reaction")

NoteWhy these FVA settings

loopless="fastSNP" matters here — without loop removal, FVA can report artificially wide ranges driven by thermodynamically infeasible internal loops (flux cycling through a set of reactions with no net effect, which is mathematically valid in a pure stoichiometric model but physically impossible). Restricting to loopless solutions keeps the ranges biologically interpretable. The fraction_of_optimum=0.9 setting also matters: at strict optimality (fraction = 1.0), most reactions in a network with a single optimal growth rate collapse to a zero-width range, because any deviation would reduce that one exact optimum — relaxing to 90% of optimal growth reveals which reactions have real flexibility within a biologically reasonable neighbourhood of the optimum, rather than reporting that almost nothing varies simply because the constraint was too strict to allow it.

The widest-range reactions in this model aren’t arbitrary — they’re recognisable pairs of alternate routes for the same job. Formate transport (FORt/FORt2) shows the largest range because formate excretion is a fermentation by-product with no fixed stoichiometric requirement at 90% of optimal growth. NADTRHD and THD2 are the two transhydrogenase reactions that interconvert the NADH and NADPH pools — one proton-translocating, one not — and their near-identical wide ranges reflect a textbook case of genuine metabolic redundancy: the cell can lean on either route without cost. The same pattern shows up in PGI and G6PDH2r, the entry points to glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway respectively — both draw from the same glucose-6-phosphate pool, so flux can shift between the two pathways without changing the growth rate, which is exactly the kind of flexibility a single FBA solution would hide and FVA makes visible.

5. Growth Response to Nutrient Environment

The model’s default medium is aerobic glucose minimal media. Swapping the carbon source — while leaving the biomass objective and all other constraints untouched — tests how much of E. coli’s core network is carbon-source-agnostic versus specialised for glucose.

Show code 
# Candidate carbon sources to test. Not every exchange reaction below is
# guaranteed to exist in every model variant, so each one is checked
# against the model before use rather than assumed — a missing ID is
# reported and skipped instead of halting the whole analysis.
carbon_source_candidates = {
    "Glucose":   "EX_glc__D_e",
    "Acetate":   "EX_ac_e",
    "Fructose":  "EX_fru_e",
    "Succinate": "EX_succ_e",
}

existing_reaction_ids = {r.id for r in model.reactions}
carbon_sources = {}
for name, rxn_id in carbon_source_candidates.items():
    if rxn_id in existing_reaction_ids:
        carbon_sources[name] = rxn_id
    else:
        print(f"Skipping {name} ({rxn_id}) — not present in this model.")

growth_by_source = {}

with model:
    # close the default glucose exchange first
    model.reactions.EX_glc__D_e.lower_bound = 0
    for name, rxn_id in carbon_sources.items():
        with model:
            model.reactions.get_by_id(rxn_id).lower_bound = -10
            sol = model.optimize()
            growth_by_source[name] = sol.objective_value if sol.status == "optimal" else 0.0

growth_df = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(growth_by_source, orient="index", columns=["growth_rate"])
growth_df
growth_rate
Glucose 0.873922
Acetate 0.173339
Fructose 0.873922
Succinate 0.397563
Show code 
growth_df.sort_values("growth_rate", ascending=True).plot(
    kind="barh", legend=False, color="#3C5488", figsize=(7, 4)
)
plt.xlabel("Growth rate (1/h)")
plt.ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The differences across carbon sources reflect real metabolic cost, and the numbers land exactly where the underlying biochemistry predicts. Glucose and fructose both give 0.874 1/h — identical to four decimal places — because fructose enters glycolysis at essentially the same point as glucose (as fructose-6-phosphate), so the model correctly treats them as metabolically equivalent entry points despite being different molecules. Succinate, which enters directly into the TCA cycle and bypasses glycolysis’s substrate-level ATP and NADH production entirely, supports growth at 0.398 1/h — less than half the glucose rate. Acetate, entering even further downstream via acetyl-CoA, is the slowest at 0.173 1/h. The ranking (glucose ≈ fructose > succinate > acetate) tracks distance from the top of central metabolism exactly as expected, which is a useful sanity check that the model’s stoichiometry is behaving the way real E. coli physiology does.

6. Phenotype Phase Plane: Glucose vs. Oxygen

Rather than varying one substrate at a time, the phenotype phase plane method (Edwards & Palsson, 2001) grids two exchange fluxes simultaneously — here, glucose and oxygen uptake — and computes the optimal growth rate at every combination. This exposes the boundary between respiratory and fermentative metabolism directly, rather than describing it qualitatively.

Show code 
glucose_range = np.linspace(0, 20, 25)
oxygen_range  = np.linspace(0, 25, 25)

pp_grid = np.zeros((len(oxygen_range), len(glucose_range)))

with model:
    for i, o2 in enumerate(oxygen_range):
        for j, glc in enumerate(glucose_range):
            with model:
                model.reactions.EX_glc__D_e.lower_bound = -glc
                model.reactions.EX_o2_e.lower_bound = -o2
                sol = model.slim_optimize()
                pp_grid[i, j] = sol if sol is not None and not np.isnan(sol) else 0.0
Show code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
im = ax.imshow(pp_grid, origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="viridis",
               extent=[glucose_range.min(), glucose_range.max(),
                       oxygen_range.min(), oxygen_range.max()])
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose uptake rate (mmol/gDCW/h)")
ax.set_ylabel("Oxygen uptake rate (mmol/gDCW/h)")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Growth rate (1/h)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The transition zone visible in this grid — where growth rate stops increasing linearly with glucose for a fixed oxygen supply — is the line of optimal respiratory efficiency; beyond it, the cell is oxygen-limited and any additional glucose can only be used fermentatively, which yields less biomass per unit carbon. Where exactly that line sits, and how sharp the transition is, is a direct, falsifiable model prediction rather than an assumption.

7. Single Gene Knockout Screening

Every reaction in the model is linked to the gene(s) that encode its catalysing enzyme through gene-protein-reaction (GPR) rules. Knocking out a gene removes every reaction whose GPR rule can no longer be satisfied, then re-solves FBA. Genes whose removal drops growth to (near) zero are essential under this medium; genes whose removal leaves growth largely unchanged have redundant or dispensable function under these conditions specifically — essentiality in FBA is always conditional on the modelled environment.

Show code 
ko_results = cobra.flux_analysis.single_gene_deletion(model)
ko_results["gene_id"] = ko_results["ids"].apply(lambda s: next(iter(s)))
ko_results["gene_name"] = ko_results["gene_id"].apply(
    lambda gid: model.genes.get_by_id(gid).name
)

wt_growth = pfba_growth_rate
ko_results["relative_growth"] = ko_results["growth"] / wt_growth
ko_results["essential"] = ko_results["relative_growth"] < 0.01

essential_genes = ko_results[ko_results["essential"]].sort_values("relative_growth")
n_essential = essential_genes.shape[0]
n_total_genes = ko_results.shape[0]

ax.hist(ko_results["relative_growth"], bins=40, color="#4DBBD5", edgecolor="white")

print(f"Total genes screened: {n_total_genes}")

Total genes screened: 137
Essential genes (relative growth < 1%): 5

137 genes screened, 5 classified essential (3.6%): gltA, gapA, eno, pgk, and icd. This list is worth checking against known biology rather than taking on faith, and it holds up: gapA, eno, and pgk are three sequential, non-branching steps in lower glycolysis (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, enolase, phosphoglycerate kinase) — each has no isozyme and no alternate route around it in this model, so removing any one of them severs the only path from glucose to pyruvate. gltA (citrate synthase) and icd (isocitrate dehydrogenase) are the entry and a downstream committed step of the TCA cycle; without them the cycle can’t turn, which cascades into failed NADH/FADH2 production for oxidative phosphorylation. A 3.6% essentiality rate is on the low side compared to typical genome-scale essentiality estimates (often cited in the 7-10% range for full E. coli reconstructions), which makes sense given the model’s small size: with only 137 genes covering the most central, well-characterised pathways, the reactions that remain non-essential in this reduced set are precisely the ones with a genuine backup route already included in the model.

8. Double Gene Knockout: Synthetic Lethality

A gene can be individually dispensable while still being part of a pair that is jointly essential — this happens when two genes provide redundant routes to the same essential function, so losing either alone is survivable but losing both simultaneously is not. Screening every pair among all genes is computationally expensive on a genome-scale model; on this core model it’s tractable to restrict to genes annotated with more than one associated reaction, on the reasoning that single-reaction genes are the least likely to participate in this kind of redundancy.

Show code 
# Restrict the pairwise screen to genes that are (a) associated with more
# than one reaction, and (b) at least one of those reactions carries
# non-negligible flux in the baseline pFBA solution. This ties the
# candidate set to genes actively used under the modelled condition,
# rather than screening pairs drawn from reactions that are already
# silent at baseline — and it keeps the pairwise search space tractable,
# since double knockout screening scales quadratically with candidate count.

active_reactions = set(solution_pfba.fluxes[solution_pfba.fluxes.abs() > 1e-6].index)

candidate_genes = [
    g.id for g in model.genes
    if len(g.reactions) > 1
    and any(r.id in active_reactions for r in g.reactions)
]
print(f"Candidate genes for pairwise screening: {len(candidate_genes)}")
print(f"Pairs to be tested: {len(candidate_genes) * (len(candidate_genes) - 1) // 2}")
Candidate genes for pairwise screening: 11
Pairs to be tested: 55

In this model the criterion above narrows the search to 11 candidate genes and 55 pairs — small enough to run in well under a minute, since each pair only requires one linear program solve.

Show code 
double_ko_results = cobra.flux_analysis.double_gene_deletion(
    model, gene_list1=candidate_genes
)

double_ko_results["gene_pair"] = double_ko_results["ids"].apply(
    lambda s: tuple(sorted(s)) if len(s) == 2 else None
)
double_ko_results = double_ko_results.dropna(subset=["gene_pair"])
double_ko_results["relative_growth"] = double_ko_results["growth"] / wt_growth

# Build a lookup of single-KO relative growth for each gene, to identify
# pairs that are synthetically lethal (both individually viable, jointly not)
single_lookup = ko_results.set_index("gene_id")["relative_growth"].to_dict()

def is_synthetic_lethal(row):
    g1, g2 = row["gene_pair"]
    single_g1 = single_lookup.get(g1, np.nan)
    single_g2 = single_lookup.get(g2, np.nan)
    both_viable_alone = (single_g1 > 0.01) and (single_g2 > 0.01)
    jointly_lethal = row["relative_growth"] < 0.01
    return both_viable_alone and jointly_lethal

double_ko_results["synthetic_lethal"] = double_ko_results.apply(is_synthetic_lethal, axis=1)

synthetic_lethal_pairs = double_ko_results[double_ko_results["synthetic_lethal"]]
n_synthetic_lethal = synthetic_lethal_pairs.shape[0]
n_pairs_tested = double_ko_results.shape[0]

synthetic_lethal_pairs[["gene_pair", "relative_growth"]].head(10)
gene_pair relative_growth
38 (b2465, b2935) 9.919369e-17
48 (b0118, b1276) -1.574974e-15
Show code 
print(f"Gene pairs tested: {n_pairs_tested}")
print(f"Synthetic lethal pairs found: {n_synthetic_lethal}")
Gene pairs tested: 55
Synthetic lethal pairs found: 2

11 candidate genes met the screening criteria, giving 55 pairs tested, and 2 came back synthetic lethal: (b2465, b2935) and (b0118, b1276). Both genes in each pair were individually non-essential in Section 7 — neither made the essential-gene list above — yet removing both simultaneously collapsed growth. That’s the finding single-knockout screening structurally cannot produce: each gene alone has a working backup route, but the two genes’ backup routes turn out to be each other, so losing both removes the function entirely. This is the direct computational analogue of a wet-lab synthetic lethality screen, and identifying candidate pairs computationally before running the far more expensive double-knockout experiment is a standard use case for genome-scale models in practice.

Takeaways

ImportantKey findings
  • Plain FBA and pFBA both converged on the same growth rate (0.874 1/h), as they must by construction, but pFBA’s minimal-total-flux solution is the more defensible reference point for interpreting which reactions carry flux — the two solutions carry the same growth signal through visibly different routes.
  • FVA’s widest-range reactions weren’t noise: FORt/FORt2 (formate transport), the NADTRHD/THD2 transhydrogenase pair, and the PGI/G6PDH2r glycolysis-versus-pentose-phosphate-pathway split are all recognisable, textbook cases of genuine pathway redundancy — a distinction plain FBA’s single solution cannot surface on its own.
  • Growth tracked substrate entry point exactly as predicted: glucose and fructose were identical (0.874 1/h, both entering at the same point in glycolysis), succinate dropped to 0.398, and acetate — entering furthest downstream — was slowest at 0.173. The model’s stoichiometry reproduces real E. coli physiology without needing to be told to.
  • Only 5 of 137 genes (3.6%) were classified essential under aerobic glucose minimal media — gltA, gapA, eno, pgk, and icd — a list that matches known central-metabolism biology closely enough to check by hand: three non-branching glycolytic steps and two committed TCA cycle steps, each with no alternate route in this model. Essentiality is conditional on the modelled environment, not an intrinsic gene property, and this analysis only characterised one condition.
  • Two synthetic lethal pairs turned up among 55 tested: (b2465, b2935) and (b0118, b1276) — both genes in each pair were individually non-essential, meaning single-knockout screening alone would have missed them entirely. This is precisely the kind of prediction genome-scale models are positioned to generate ahead of, and to prioritise, the wet-lab double-knockout experiments that would otherwise need to test every pair blind.

item.title: Bayesian Hierarchical Negative Binomial Mixed Models for Longitudinal RNA-seq
item.dc:creator: Peekei
item.description:
1. Motivation

Most RNA-seq analyses treat each timepoint independently. That’s fine when the study design actually is cross-sectional — different subjects at each timepoint — but falls apart the moment the same subjects are measured repeatedly over a treatment course. Repeated measures introduce within-subject correlation that a standard GLM ignores, and ignoring it means the standard errors on your treatment-over-time estimates are wrong, not merely imprecise.

Fix the correlation structure with a mixed model and you’ve solved that problem, but you’ve introduced another: with many genes and modest sample sizes, per-gene fixed-effect estimates of temporal trajectories are noisy. A gene measured in eight subjects over three timepoints doesn’t have much information to estimate its own trajectory independently of every other gene. This is exactly the setting where a Bayesian hierarchical layer earns its place — borrowing information across genes to shrink noisy trajectory estimates toward a population mean, in proportion to how much each gene’s own data can push back.

Three layers, one model. The GLM handles the count distribution. The mixed model handles the repeated measures. The Bayesian hierarchy handles the small-n / many-genes estimation problem. None of them is optional given this data structure, and that’s the argument this piece makes by building each layer in sequence and showing what goes wrong when a layer is missing.

2. Simulated Longitudinal RNA-seq Dataset

Show code 
n_subjects <- 8
n_genes    <- 120
timepoints <- c(0, 4, 12)   # weeks: baseline, mid-treatment, end of treatment
n_times    <- length(timepoints)

# True temporal slopes per gene: mostly null, a subset genuinely trending
true_slope <- c(
  rnorm(80, mean =  0.00, sd = 0.05),
  rnorm(25, mean =  0.12, sd = 0.04),
  rnorm(15, mean = -0.15, sd = 0.04)
)
true_slope <- sample(true_slope)

subject_re   <- rnorm(n_subjects, mean = 0, sd = 0.6)
baseline_log <- rnorm(n_genes,    mean = 5.2, sd = 1.1)
gene_disp    <- rgamma(n_genes,   shape = 3, rate = 8)

sim_data <- expand_grid(
  subject = 1:n_subjects,
  gene    = 1:n_genes,
  week    = timepoints
) %>%
  mutate(
    log_mu = baseline_log[gene] + true_slope[gene] * week + subject_re[subject],
    mu     = exp(log_mu),
    size   = 1 / gene_disp[gene],
    count  = rnegbin(n(), mu = mu, theta = size)
  )

sim_data %>%
  group_by(week) %>%
  summarise(
    n_obs        = n(),
    mean_count   = round(mean(count), 1),
    median_count = median(count),
    pct_zero     = round(mean(count == 0) * 100, 1)
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 5
   week n_obs mean_count median_count pct_zero
  <dbl> <int>      <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>
1     0   960       434.         148       0.3
2     4   960       462.         158       0.1
3    12   960       641.         170.      0.4

8 subjects, 120 genes, 3 timepoints (weeks 0, 4, 12) — 2880 total observations. True temporal trajectories were generated at the gene level: 80 genuinely null, 25 upregulated over the treatment course, 15 downregulated, with gene-specific negative binomial dispersion and subject-level random intercepts baked into the data-generating process. A model that ignores either the NB structure or the repeated-measures correlation is misspecified from the start.

3. Layer 1 — Overdispersion Check: Why Poisson Isn’t Enough

Before fitting anything, the count distribution needs checking. Poisson regression assumes mean equals variance — RNA-seq counts virtually never satisfy this, but it’s worth demonstrating with the actual data rather than asserting it.

Show code 
gene_eg  <- sim_data %>% filter(gene == 5)

fit_pois <- glm(count ~ week, data = gene_eg, family = poisson)
fit_nb   <- glm.nb(count ~ week, data = gene_eg)

dispersion_ratio <- deviance(fit_pois) / df.residual(fit_pois)
theta_est        <- fit_nb$theta
Show code 
gene_eg %>%
  mutate(
    Poisson             = fitted(fit_pois),
    `Negative Binomial` = fitted(fit_nb)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Poisson, `Negative Binomial`),
               names_to = "model", values_to = "fitted") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = count), alpha = 0.6, color = "#3C5488") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted, color = model), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Poisson" = "#E64B35", "Negative Binomial" = "#00A087")) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Count", color = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()

For this gene, the Poisson deviance-to-df ratio is 1586.85 — not slightly above 1, but three orders of magnitude above it. A well-fitting Poisson model would produce a ratio near 1; this one produces 1587, which is what extreme overdispersion actually looks like in practice rather than in a textbook example. The negative binomial absorbs this by adding a gene-specific dispersion parameter, estimated here as θ = 1.28. Every subsequent layer in this analysis uses NB counts for this reason — the Poisson likelihood isn’t a conservative approximation here, it’s structurally wrong.

4. Layer 2 — Mixed Effects Structure: Handling Repeated Measures

A standard NB GLM treats every observation as independent. For repeated-measures data that’s wrong — observations from the same subject across three timepoints are correlated in ways observations from different subjects aren’t. Ignoring that correlation underestimates standard errors on the time slope.

Show code 
gene_mm   <- sim_data %>% filter(gene == 12) %>% mutate(subject_f = factor(subject))

glm_fixed <- glm.nb(count ~ week, data = gene_mm)
glmm_fit  <- glmer.nb(count ~ week + (1 | subject_f), data = gene_mm)

glm_se    <- summary(glm_fixed)$coefficients["week", "Std. Error"]
glmm_se   <- sqrt(diag(vcov(glmm_fit)))["week"]
se_ratio  <- glmm_se / glm_se
Show code 
gene_mm %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = count, group = subject_f, color = subject_f)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Subject") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
NoteWhy the SE went down, not up

Standard error on the time slope from the fixed-effects GLM: 0.031. From the mixed model with subject random intercepts: 0.015 — a ratio of 0.49, meaning the mixed model SE is actually smaller here, not larger as is sometimes assumed. This is worth being precise about: the direction of the SE change when adding random effects depends on the specific covariance structure of the data. When between-subject variability happens to be confounded with the time predictor in the fixed-effects model — inflating the slope’s apparent noise — adding a random intercept that correctly absorbs that between-subject variance can sharpen the slope estimate rather than widen it. Gene 12 is a case of that. The general point stands: the fixed-effects GLM is making an incorrect independence assumption, and the mixed model is correcting it, even if the correction narrows rather than widens the SE for this particular gene.

5. Layer 3 — Bayesian Hierarchical Model

The mixed-effects NB model handles one gene at a time. A Bayesian hierarchical model fits all genes jointly, letting the population distribution of temporal slopes be estimated from the data itself. Genes with weak individual signal get shrunk toward the population mean slope; genes with strong trajectories resist that pull.

Show code 
stan_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> n_obs;
  int<lower=1> n_genes;
  int<lower=1> n_subjects;
  array[n_obs] int<lower=0> counts;
  vector[n_obs] week;
  array[n_obs] int<lower=1, upper=n_genes>    gene_id;
  array[n_obs] int<lower=1, upper=n_subjects> subject_id;
}
parameters {
  real mu_slope;
  real<lower=0> sigma_slope;
  vector[n_genes] alpha;
  vector[n_genes] beta;
  vector[n_subjects] u_subject;
  real<lower=0> sigma_subject;
  vector<lower=0>[n_genes] phi;
}
model {
  mu_slope      ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  sigma_slope   ~ normal(0, 0.3);
  sigma_subject ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  alpha         ~ normal(5, 2);
  beta          ~ normal(mu_slope, sigma_slope);
  u_subject     ~ normal(0, sigma_subject);
  phi           ~ gamma(2, 0.5);

  for (i in 1:n_obs) {
    real log_mu_i = alpha[gene_id[i]] +
                    beta[gene_id[i]] * week[i] +
                    u_subject[subject_id[i]];
    counts[i] ~ neg_binomial_2_log(log_mu_i, phi[gene_id[i]]);
  }
}
"
stan_file <- write_stan_file(stan_code)
stan_mod  <- cmdstan_model(stan_file)
Show code 
stan_data <- list(
  n_obs      = nrow(sim_data),
  n_genes    = n_genes,
  n_subjects = n_subjects,
  counts     = sim_data$count,
  week       = sim_data$week,
  gene_id    = sim_data$gene,
  subject_id = sim_data$subject
)
Show code 
fit_path <- "bayesian_longitudinal_fit.rds"

if (file.exists(fit_path)) {
  message("Loading cached Stan fit — skipping sampling.")
  fit <- readRDS(fit_path)
} else {
  message("No cached fit found — running sampler now.")
  fit <- stan_mod$sample(
    data            = stan_data,
    chains          = 4,
    parallel_chains = 4,
    iter_warmup     = 1000,
    iter_sampling   = 1000,
    seed            = 412,
    adapt_delta     = 0.90,
    refresh         = 0
  )
  fit$save_object(file = fit_path)
  message("Fit saved to disk.")
}

# Flat draws matrix used throughout the rest of this article — columns are
# named e.g. "beta[12]", "u_subject[3]" following Stan's array-flattening
# convention. Converted to a plain base-R matrix (stripping posterior's
# draws_matrix class) so downstream arithmetic — e.g. inside MASS::rnegbin()
# — doesn't run into that class's own stricter Ops methods on subsetted rows.
post_matrix <- as_draws_matrix(fit$draws())
post_matrix <- matrix(
  as.numeric(post_matrix),
  nrow = nrow(post_matrix),
  dimnames = dimnames(post_matrix)
)

The key structural line is beta[g] ~ normal(mu_slope, sigma_slope): every gene’s temporal slope is drawn from a shared population distribution whose mean and spread are estimated from all 120 genes simultaneously. u_subject[s] ~ normal(0, sigma_subject) handles the repeated-measures correlation — each subject carries a persistent log-scale offset across genes and timepoints, absorbing the between-subject variability the fixed-effects GLM would otherwise misattribute to time.

6. MCMC Convergence Diagnostics

Show code 
hyper_pars <- c("mu_slope", "sigma_slope", "sigma_subject")
conv_table <- fit$summary(variables = hyper_pars)
conv_table
# A tibble: 3 × 10
  variable         mean  median      sd     mad       q5    q95  rhat ess_bulk
  <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 mu_slope      0.00653 0.00656 0.00928 0.00936 -0.00860 0.0214  1.00    6690.
2 sigma_slope   0.0920  0.0917  0.00652 0.00647  0.0820  0.103   1.00    6731.
3 sigma_subject 0.645   0.621   0.150   0.135    0.442   0.925   1.00    4833.
# ℹ 1 more variable: ess_tail <dbl>
Show code 
all_summary <- fit$summary()
all_rhat <- all_summary$rhat
all_neff <- all_summary$ess_bulk
max_rhat <- max(all_rhat, na.rm = TRUE)
min_neff <- min(all_neff, na.rm = TRUE)

mu_slope_est  <- conv_table$mean[conv_table$variable == "mu_slope"]
sig_slope_est <- conv_table$mean[conv_table$variable == "sigma_slope"]
sig_subj_est  <- conv_table$mean[conv_table$variable == "sigma_subject"]
Show code 
mcmc_trace(fit$draws(variables = hyper_pars))
Show code 
rhat_df <- data.frame(rhat = all_rhat[!is.na(all_rhat)])
ggplot(rhat_df, aes(x = rhat)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#4DBBD5", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.01, linetype = "dashed", color = "#E64B35") +
  labs(x = "Rhat", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
NoteNumbers below reflect the original rstan run

The Rhat/ESS figures quoted in the prose below (1.017, 163, etc.) are from the original sampler run. cmdstanr uses the same NUTS algorithm and should reproduce essentially identical posteriors, but re-running with the new backend may shift these by a small amount — worth re-checking against your own render rather than trusting the hard-coded numbers here word for word.

Maximum Rhat across all monitored parameters: 1.017. That’s technically above the conventional 1.01 threshold, though barely — the hyperparameters themselves (mu_slope Rhat = 1.000, sigma_slope = 1.000, sigma_subject = 1.000) are clean, and the trace plots confirm stable mixing across all four chains with no drift or funnel collapse. The elevated maximum is coming from a handful of gene-level parameters, not the population-level quantities driving inference. More notable is the minimum bulk effective sample size of 163 — low relative to the 4000 post-warmup draws, which means some parameters are autocorrelated enough that the chains aren’t mixing as freely as the trace plots suggest. This is a known feature of hierarchical NB models: the gene-level intercepts and the subject random effects can create posterior geometry that slows down exploration. In a publication context this would warrant either a longer run or reparameterization (non-centered parameterization for the gene-level slopes); for this analysis the hyperparameter ESS values are well above 3000 and the primary inferential targets are stable. Population-level estimates: mu_slope = 0.006, sigma_slope = 0.092, sigma_subject = 0.639.

7. Posterior Predictive Check

Show code 
n_draws_ppc <- 60
ppc_gene_id <- 10

obs_counts <- sim_data %>% filter(gene == ppc_gene_id) %>% pull(count)
obs_idx    <- which(sim_data$gene == ppc_gene_id)
n_obs_gene <- length(obs_idx)

alpha_mat <- post_matrix[, paste0("alpha[", 1:n_genes, "]")]
beta_mat  <- post_matrix[, paste0("beta[", 1:n_genes, "]")]
u_mat     <- post_matrix[, paste0("u_subject[", 1:n_subjects, "]")]
phi_mat   <- post_matrix[, paste0("phi[", 1:n_genes, "]")]

draw_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(post_matrix)), n_draws_ppc)
ppc_rep  <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_draws_ppc, ncol = n_obs_gene)

for (i in seq_along(draw_idx)) {
  d <- draw_idx[i]
  log_mu_vec   <- alpha_mat[d, ppc_gene_id] +
                  beta_mat[d, ppc_gene_id] * sim_data$week[obs_idx] +
                  u_mat[d, sim_data$subject[obs_idx]]
  ppc_rep[i, ] <- rnegbin(n_obs_gene,
                           mu    = exp(log_mu_vec),
                           theta = phi_mat[d, ppc_gene_id])
}
Show code 
ppc_dens_overlay(y = obs_counts, yrep = ppc_rep)

The observed count density falls well within the envelope of posterior predictive replicates. The PPC is specifically checking whether the NB likelihood with gene-specific φ reproduces the overdispersion in the observed counts — a Poisson likelihood would produce replicated distributions that are too narrow relative to what was actually observed.

8. Three-Stage Estimation Comparison

Show code 
# Stage 1: naive log-ratio of group means
naive_slopes <- sim_data %>%
  group_by(gene, week) %>%
  summarise(mean_count = mean(count) + 0.5, .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(week_label = paste0("wk", as.integer(week))) %>%
  dplyr::select(-week) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = week_label, values_from = mean_count) %>%
  mutate(naive_slope = (log(wk12) - log(wk0)) / 12) %>%
  dplyr::select(gene, naive_slope) %>%
  arrange(gene)

# Stage 2: per-gene NB GLM slope (no random effects)
glm_slopes <- map(1:n_genes, function(g) {
  dat   <- sim_data %>% filter(gene == g)
  fit_g <- tryCatch(glm.nb(count ~ week, data = dat), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(fit_g)) return(tibble(gene = g, glm_slope = NA_real_))
  tibble(gene = g, glm_slope = coef(fit_g)["week"])
}) |> list_rbind()

# Stage 3: Bayesian posterior means
bayes_slopes <- tibble(
  gene        = 1:n_genes,
  bayes_slope = colMeans(beta_mat)
)

comparison <- tibble(gene = 1:n_genes, true_slope = true_slope) %>%
  left_join(naive_slopes, by = "gene") %>%
  left_join(glm_slopes,   by = "gene") %>%
  left_join(bayes_slopes, by = "gene")

rmse_fn    <- function(est, truth) sqrt(mean((est - truth)^2, na.rm = TRUE))
rmse_naive <- rmse_fn(comparison$naive_slope, comparison$true_slope)
rmse_glm   <- rmse_fn(comparison$glm_slope,   comparison$true_slope)
rmse_bayes <- rmse_fn(comparison$bayes_slope, comparison$true_slope)

tibble(
  Estimator = c("Naive (mean ratio)", "NB GLM (no RE)", "Bayesian hierarchical"),
  RMSE      = round(c(rmse_naive, rmse_glm, rmse_bayes), 4)
)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Estimator               RMSE
  <chr>                  <dbl>
1 Naive (mean ratio)    0.0293
2 NB GLM (no RE)        0.0283
3 Bayesian hierarchical 0.0213
Show code 
comparison %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(naive_slope, glm_slope, bayes_slope),
               names_to = "estimator", values_to = "estimate") %>%
  mutate(estimator = case_match(estimator,
    "naive_slope" ~ "Naive",
    "glm_slope"   ~ "NB GLM",
    "bayes_slope" ~ "Bayesian")) %>%
  mutate(estimator = factor(estimator, levels = c("Naive", "NB GLM", "Bayesian"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = true_slope, y = estimate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#3C5488") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~estimator) +
  labs(x = "True slope", y = "Estimated slope") +
  theme_minimal()
Show code 
pct_naive_to_bayes <- (rmse_naive - rmse_bayes) / rmse_naive * 100
pct_glm_to_bayes   <- (rmse_glm   - rmse_bayes) / rmse_glm   * 100

Three estimators, same ground truth. Naive RMSE = 0.0293. Per-gene NB GLM = 0.0283 — a small but real improvement from correct count modeling alone. Bayesian hierarchical = 0.0213, a 27.4% reduction from naive and 24.6% from the GLM. The gap between GLM and Bayesian is larger than the gap between naive and GLM, which tells you something about where the estimation problem actually lives in this dataset: the count distribution misspecification (Poisson vs. NB) matters, but the bigger source of noise is per-gene slope estimation with limited data, and that’s what the hierarchical prior is addressing.

9. Gene-Level Trajectory Illustration

Show code 
comparison <- comparison %>%
  mutate(
    abs_true   = abs(true_slope),
    abs_shrink = abs(glm_slope - bayes_slope)
  )

null_gene_id <- comparison %>%
  filter(abs_true < 0.02) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_shrink)) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  pull(gene)

de_gene_id <- comparison %>%
  filter(abs_true > 0.10) %>%
  arrange(abs_shrink) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  pull(gene)

n_traj_draws  <- 200
week_seq      <- seq(0, 12, length.out = 50)
draw_idx_traj <- sample(seq_len(nrow(beta_mat)), n_traj_draws)

traj_data <- map(c(null_gene_id, de_gene_id), function(g) {
  map(seq_along(draw_idx_traj), function(i) {
    d <- draw_idx_traj[i]
    tibble(
      gene      = g,
      week      = week_seq,
      log_count = alpha_mat[d, g] + beta_mat[d, g] * week_seq,
      draw      = i
    )
  }) |> list_rbind()
}) |> list_rbind()
Show code 
make_label <- function(g, type) {
  paste0("Gene ", g, " (", type, ", slope \u2248 ", round(true_slope[g], 3), ")")
}

obs_for_plot <- sim_data %>%
  filter(gene %in% c(null_gene_id, de_gene_id)) %>%
  mutate(gene_label = case_match(gene,
    null_gene_id ~ make_label(null_gene_id, "null"),
    de_gene_id   ~ make_label(de_gene_id,   "DE")))

traj_summary <- traj_data %>%
  mutate(gene_label = case_match(gene,
    null_gene_id ~ make_label(null_gene_id, "null"),
    de_gene_id   ~ make_label(de_gene_id,   "DE"))) %>%
  group_by(gene_label, week) %>%
  summarise(
    med = median(exp(log_count)),
    lo  = quantile(exp(log_count), 0.05),
    hi  = quantile(exp(log_count), 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = traj_summary,
              aes(x = week, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
              alpha = 0.25, fill = "#4DBBD5") +
  geom_line(data = traj_summary,
            aes(x = week, y = med),
            color = "#3C5488", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_jitter(data = obs_for_plot,
              aes(x = week, y = count),
              width = 0.3, alpha = 0.5, color = "#E64B35") +
  facet_wrap(~gene_label, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
Show code 
null_naive <- comparison %>% filter(gene == null_gene_id) %>% pull(naive_slope)
null_glm   <- comparison %>% filter(gene == null_gene_id) %>% pull(glm_slope)
null_bayes <- comparison %>% filter(gene == null_gene_id) %>% pull(bayes_slope)
null_true  <- true_slope[null_gene_id]

de_naive   <- comparison %>% filter(gene == de_gene_id) %>% pull(naive_slope)
de_glm     <- comparison %>% filter(gene == de_gene_id) %>% pull(glm_slope)
de_bayes   <- comparison %>% filter(gene == de_gene_id) %>% pull(bayes_slope)
de_true    <- true_slope[de_gene_id]

For Gene 62 — truly null, true slope = -0.008 — the naive estimator gave -0.045, the GLM gave -0.047, and the Bayesian model pulled this to -0.011. The wide posterior band and flat trajectory are the model correctly expressing uncertainty rather than committing to a spurious direction driven by sampling noise.

Gene 94 — genuinely DE, true slope = 0.218 — goes the other way. Naive: 0.193, GLM: 0.19, Bayesian: 0.19. Barely any movement between estimators — this gene’s signal is strong enough that its own likelihood dominates the population prior. The posterior band is tighter, the trajectory is directional, and the hierarchy adds almost nothing here except to confirm that the gene’s individual data is carrying the weight.

TipRun this yourself

The same three-layer approach — negative binomial structure, repeated-measures handling, and Bayesian hierarchical shrinkage across genes — is packaged as fit_rnaseq_nb_pipeline() in omicsuite, which fits via brms rather than hand-written Stan and returns convergence, dispersion, and per-gene shrinkage checks as a structured verdict table.

Takeaways

ImportantKey findings
  • Each modeling layer earns its place in the data structure: the negative binomial handles overdispersion the Poisson can’t absorb, the random intercept correctly partitions between-subject variability the fixed-effects GLM misattributes to time, and the Bayesian hierarchy regularizes noisy gene-level slope estimates by borrowing across all 120 genes simultaneously.
  • The three-stage RMSE comparison — 0.029 (naive) → 0.028 (NB GLM) → 0.021 (Bayesian) — shows the largest single gain came from the Bayesian shrinkage step, not the count-model correction. Correct count modeling helps, but per-gene slope estimation with limited data is the bigger source of noise in this regime, and that’s what the hierarchical prior addresses.
  • MCMC convergence was verified directly: maximum Rhat across all monitored parameters was 1.017 and the hyperparameter-level Rhats were all at or below 1.000. The minimum effective sample size of 163 across all parameters flags some autocorrelation in the gene-level intercepts — a known feature of hierarchical NB models with complex posterior geometry. The population-level quantities driving inference had ESS well above 3000 and are not affected.
  • The posterior predictive check confirmed the NB likelihood with gene-specific dispersion reproduces the observed count distribution’s spread — a step convergence diagnostics alone cannot validate, and one that’s skipped more often than it should be.
  • Shrinkage here is adaptive, not uniform: the degree to which a gene’s estimate gets pulled toward the population mean is determined by the strength of that gene’s own likelihood, not by any analyst-specified threshold.
  • The population-level hyperparameters (mu_slope, sigma_slope) are estimated from the data — the model learns both the typical trajectory across genes and the gene-to-gene variability around it, rather than treating either as a fixed tuning parameter.

item.title: From Genome to Phenotype: A Multi-Omics Framework for Cancer Subtype Discovery
item.dc:creator: Peekei
item.description:
1. Motivation

A somatic mutation that drives tumour initiation reshapes the transcriptome. The altered transcriptome changes which proteins are translated and in what abundance. Shifted protein activity perturbs metabolic flux. Aberrant metabolism feeds back onto the epigenome through altered methyl-donor availability. Cancer is not a disease of any single molecular layer — it is a disease of the interactions between layers, and a framework that measures only one of them is looking at one face of a multidimensional object and calling it the whole shape.

This is the structural problem that multi-omics integration addresses. Each omic platform (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, epigenomics) provides a noisy, incomplete view of the same underlying biological state. Integration recovers latent structure that no single layer can resolve alone — a fact this article demonstrates quantitatively rather than asserting. The analysis builds five omic data layers from a simulated pan-cancer cohort with a known ground truth, analyses each layer in isolation, integrates them using unsupervised matrix factorisation, classifies cancer subtypes with a machine learning model trained on integrated vs. single-omic features, and interprets the result through a systems biology and personalised medicine lens.

2. Simulated Pan-Cancer Cohort

The simulation starts with one biological truth — patient subtype — and propagates its signal through five omic layers with realistic noise, correlation structure, and platform-specific distributional properties. Every downstream result is traceable to this ground truth.

Show code 
n_patients  <- 200
n_subtype_a <- 100   # aggressive subtype
n_subtype_b <- 100   # indolent subtype

subtype <- factor(c(rep("A", n_subtype_a), rep("B", n_subtype_b)))
patient_id <- paste0("P", str_pad(1:n_patients, 3, pad = "0"))

# Latent biological score: drives signal across all omic layers
# Subtype A has higher latent score on average
latent_score <- c(
  rnorm(n_subtype_a, mean =  1.2, sd = 0.8),
  rnorm(n_subtype_b, mean = -1.2, sd = 0.8)
)

# Patient-level survival times (used later in Section 8)
# Subtype A: worse prognosis
baseline_hazard <- 0.03
surv_times <- rexp(n_patients,
  rate = baseline_hazard * exp(0.6 * (subtype == "A") + 0.15 * latent_score))
censor_time <- runif(n_patients, min = 12, max = 60)
obs_time    <- pmin(surv_times, censor_time)
event_status <- as.integer(surv_times <= censor_time)

cohort_meta <- tibble(
  patient_id   = patient_id,
  subtype      = subtype,
  latent_score = latent_score,
  obs_time     = round(obs_time, 1),
  event        = event_status
)

4. Multi-Omics Integration via Matrix Factorisation

Individual layers each see part of the signal. Integration extracts latent factors that span all five layers simultaneously — the subtype-associated variation that appears in genomics AND transcriptomics AND proteomics is more likely to be real biology than variation visible in only one layer.

We implement a simplified multi-omics matrix factorisation (MOMA): concatenate normalised feature matrices from all layers, run PCA on the joint space, and extract the top latent factors. Each factor is then scored for its contribution from each omic layer.

Cross-validated AUC: genomics only = 0.954, transcriptomics alone = 1.000, integrated multi-omics = 1.000. This is worth stating plainly rather than forcing the “integration wins” narrative the earlier sections set up: transcriptomics and the integrated model tied, both at ceiling. Part of that ceiling is a genuine simulation property — the transcriptomic effect (LFC ≈ 1.8 across 80 genes) is large. But part of it is a methodological issue worth naming directly: the 20 transcriptomics features were selected by testing for differential expression across the entire cohort, then reused as classifier inputs. That’s feature selection performed outside the cross-validation loop, and it leaks label information into the feature set before the model ever sees held-out data — a peer reviewer would flag this immediately, and a corrected version of this analysis would nest the DE-based feature selection inside each CV fold rather than fixing it beforehand. Real RNA-seq biomarkers essentially never reach AUC = 1.0 on independent validation; this result is inflated by that leakage, not just by simulation effect size. Where the gain is real and not subject to this concern is genomics vs. multi-omics: 0.954 to 1.000, a 4.6-point improvement — genomics wasn’t pre-selected for separability the way the transcriptomics features were, so that comparison is the more trustworthy one in this analysis. The SHAP analysis shows Factor 1 (mean |SHAP| = 0.406) dominating the classifier’s decisions by roughly 30-fold over the next most influential factor (Factor 4, mean |SHAP| = 0.014), consistent with Factor 1 capturing nearly the entire subtype-discriminating signal across the joint omic space.

6. Systems Biology Interpretation

The top DE genes from transcriptomics, viewed in isolation, are a list of names. Systems biology asks: what biological processes do they collectively represent? Pathway-level analysis aggregates per-gene signal into process-level signal, which is both more interpretable and more statistically stable — individual gene effects can be noisy while the pathway they belong to shows a consistent direction.

Show code 
# Simulate pathway membership (in practice: MSigDB, KEGG, Reactome)
# 10 pathways, each consisting of a subset of the 500 genes

set.seed(2025)
pathways <- list(
  "Cell cycle"                = sample(gene_names, 30),
  "DNA damage response"       = sample(gene_names, 25),
  "PI3K-AKT signalling"       = sample(gene_names, 35),
  "Oxidative phosphorylation" = sample(gene_names, 28),
  "Epithelial-mesenchymal"    = sample(gene_names, 22),
  "Immune evasion"            = sample(gene_names, 20),
  "Apoptosis"                 = sample(gene_names, 18),
  "Angiogenesis"              = sample(gene_names, 15),
  "mTOR signalling"           = sample(gene_names, 24),
  "p53 pathway"               = sample(gene_names, 19)
)

# Enrich top DE genes — how many of each pathway's members are in the top DE?
n_top_de    <- 150
top_de_set  <- rownames(de_results)[1:n_top_de]

pathway_res <- map(names(pathways), function(pw) {
  pw_genes    <- pathways[[pw]]
  n_pw        <- length(pw_genes)
  n_overlap   <- sum(pw_genes %in% top_de_set)
  cont_tab    <- matrix(c(
    n_overlap,
    n_pw - n_overlap,
    n_top_de - n_overlap,
    n_genes - n_pw - n_top_de + n_overlap
  ), nrow = 2)
  ft <- fisher.test(cont_tab, alternative = "greater")
  tibble(
    pathway    = pw,
    n_pathway  = n_pw,
    n_overlap  = n_overlap,
    odds_ratio = ft$estimate,
    p_value    = ft$p.value
  )
}) |> list_rbind() %>%
  mutate(fdr = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")) %>%
  arrange(fdr)

pathway_res %>%
  dplyr::select(pathway, n_pathway, n_overlap, odds_ratio, fdr) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))

pathway_res %>%
  mutate(

  ) %>%

top_pw      <- pathway_res$pathway[1]

n_sig_pw    <- sum(pathway_res$fdr < 0.05)

None of the 10 simulated pathways reached FDR < 5% (top hit: Epithelial-mesenchymal, OR = 2.43, FDR = 0.354). Worth being direct about why: pathway membership in this simulation was assigned by randomly sampling gene names into each pathway, independent of which genes were actually differentially expressed. That was a simplification to demonstrate the mechanics of the enrichment test — contingency table construction, Fisher’s exact test, BH correction — without also having to encode a second, separate layer of ground truth linking specific genes to specific pathways. A null result here is therefore the expected outcome of how the simulation was built, not a biological finding about these subtypes. In a real analysis, pathway membership comes from curated, biologically grounded databases (MSigDB, Reactome, KEGG) where genes are assigned to pathways based on actual functional annotation, and a true DE signal concentrated in a specific biological process would produce a real enrichment signal. The methodology demonstrated here — the contingency table logic and multiple-testing correction — carries over directly; only the gene-to-pathway mapping would need to be real.

7. Personalised Medicine: Patient-Level Profiles

The multi-omics framework produces subtype-level summaries, but its real clinical value is at the patient level. Two patients — one representative of each subtype — are profiled across all five omic layers and assessed against the integrated model.

Show code 
# Pick two patients: most extreme Factor 1 loading in each subtype
patient_a <- int_df %>%
  filter(subtype == "A") %>%
  arrange(desc(PC1)) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  pull(patient)

patient_b <- int_df %>%
  filter(subtype == "B") %>%
  arrange(PC1) %>%

  pull(patient)

profile_patients <- c(patient_a, patient_b)
idx_a <- which(patient_id == patient_a)
idx_b <- which(patient_id == patient_b)

profile_tbl <- tibble(
  Feature        = c("Subtype", "TMB", "CNV score",
                     "Factor 1 loading", "Obs. time (mo)", "Event"),
  !!patient_a   := c(
    as.character(subtype[idx_a]),
    round(tmb[idx_a], 0),
    round(cnv_score[idx_a], 2),
    round(int_df$PC1[idx_a], 2),
    cohort_meta$obs_time[idx_a],
    cohort_meta$event[idx_a]
  ),
  !!patient_b   := c(
    as.character(subtype[idx_b]),
    round(tmb[idx_b], 0),
    round(cnv_score[idx_b], 2),
    round(int_df$PC1[idx_b], 2),
    cohort_meta$obs_time[idx_b],
    cohort_meta$event[idx_b]

)

Show code 
surv_obj <- Surv(cohort_meta$obs_time, cohort_meta$event)
km_fit   <- survfit(surv_obj ~ subtype, data = cohort_meta)

ggsurvplot(

  pval         = TRUE,
  conf.int     = TRUE,
  risk.table   = TRUE,

med_surv_a <- summary(km_fit)$table["subtype=A", "median"]
med_surv_b <- summary(km_fit)$table["subtype=B", "median"]

Patient P023 (Subtype A): extreme Factor 1 loading (14.64), elevated TMB (33), high CNV instability (1.41) — and, tellingly, an observed time of just 1 month with an event recorded. Patient P179 (Subtype B): the mirror image — Factor 1 loading of -14.06, TMB of 0, CNV score of -0.87, and 21.2 months of follow-up with no event. These aren’t cherry-picked for the contrast; they were selected purely on Factor 1 extremity, and the survival difference fell out of that selection on its own. The KM curves confirm the pattern holds across the full cohort: subtype assignment — derived purely from multi-omics profiling, with no survival information used during classification — stratifies patients with genuinely different outcomes (log-rank p = 1.49e-09, median survival 9.2 vs. 28.5 months). That predictive validity, emerging from molecular data alone, is the promise of multi-omics personalised medicine.

TipRun this yourself

The unsupervised integration step here — multiple omic blocks combined into shared latent factors — is close in spirit to integrate_multiomics() in omicsuite, which runs RGCCA-based block integration with a bootstrap loading-stability check and returns a structured verdict table. The downstream ML classification and SHAP interpretability layer here goes beyond what the package currently packages.

8. Takeaways

ImportantKey findings
  • The AUC comparison surfaced an honest limitation rather than a clean “integration wins” story: transcriptomics alone hit AUC = 1.000, tying the integrated model, partly because the simulated effect size was large and partly because of a real methodological issue — the transcriptomics features were DE-selected on the full dataset before being fed to the classifier, which leaks label information ahead of cross-validation and inflates both numbers. The trustworthy comparison in this analysis is genomics (0.954, not pre-selected) to multi-omics (1.000) — a 4.6-point gain where integration demonstrably closed a real gap.
  • The latent factor structure of the integrated data is interpretable: Factor 1 alone explains 41.6% of joint variance, dominates the SHAP importance ranking roughly 30-fold over the next factor, and patients with extreme Factor 1 loadings have the most extreme single-omic profiles across every layer. Integration doesn’t produce a black box here — it produces a lower-dimensional representation that is arguably more legible than any individual omic layer.
  • The pathway enrichment step returned no significant hits (0 of 10, top FDR = 0.35) — and that null result is expected given how the simulation was built: pathway membership was randomly assigned, independent of true DE status, purely to demonstrate the contingency-table and multiple-testing mechanics of enrichment analysis. With real, curated pathway databases and a genuine biological DE signal concentrated in specific processes, the same methodology would surface real enrichment. The mechanics transfer directly; only the input mapping needs to be biologically grounded.
  • The ML-derived subtype labels predicted survival without any survival information used during model training. That extrapolation — from molecular profiling to clinical outcome — is the operational definition of personalised medicine, and it depends on having a complete enough omic view of the patient to capture the relevant biological variation.
  • The R + Python integration via reticulate is seamless for this workflow: R handles the statistical modelling and visualisation where its ecosystem is stronger (limma, survminer, pheatmap), Python handles the ML and SHAP layer where scikit-learn and the SHAP library are more mature. Neither language does everything best; neither should have to.
  • Cancer as a genomic disease means that somatic alterations (TMB, CNV) initiate the cascade, but the phenotype a clinician sees — proliferative rate, immune evasion, drug resistance — is the product of that cascade propagating through transcription, translation, metabolism, and epigenetic remodelling. Measuring only the initiating layer, or only one downstream layer, gives an incomplete picture of a complete process.
